thread.title: Apple wants to pump $350 billion into U.S. economy, build new corporate campus

author: Janice Bitters
title: Apple wants to pump $350 billion into U.S. economy, build new corporate campus
text: – Houston Business Journal Jan 17, 2018, 3:50pm CST Apple Inc . (Nasdaq: AAPL) is gearing up to build another corporate campus in a yet-to-be-announced American city and increase its workforce across the U.S. by 20,000 employees over the next five years, the iPhone maker said Jan. 17. The news was packaged with Apple’s announcement that it plans to invest $350 billion in the U.S. economy between now and the end of 2023. After the company's California headquarters, the next-largest Apple campus is actually in Texas. Austin is home to more than 6,000 Apple employees, so it's already a major corporate hub for the tech giant. It stands to reason some of those billions could land in the Texas capital; CEO Tim Cook said during an August visit that the company will continue to grow there . Additionally, some prominent economic forecasters such as Angelos Angelou have predicted Apple's workforce in Central Texas could someday surpass that of Dell Technologies Inc. , long the most-dominant technology employer in the region. Apple says its $350 billion investment will come through increased spending in manufacturing, capital expenditures, hiring, product sales and company and employee tax payments, including about $38 billion in repatriation tax payments as part of recent changes to tax laws. “Apple is a success story that could only have happened in America, and we are proud to build on our long history of support for the U.S. economy,” Apple CEO Tim Cook said in a statement. “We believe deeply in the power of American ingenuity, and we are focusing our investments in areas where we can have a direct impact on job creation and job preparedness. We have a deep sense of responsibility to give back to our country and the people who help make our success possible.” In an interview with the Wall Street Journal last year , President Donald Trump said he’d had conversation with Cook in which the CEO promised that the iPhone maker would build “three big plants, beautiful plants” in the U.S. “I spoke to [Mr. Cook], he’s promised me three big plants — big, big, big,” Trump told the WSJ in July 2017. “I said you know, Tim, unless you start building your plants in this country, I won’t consider my administration an economic success. He called me, and he said they are going forward.” The president didn't elaborate on where they would be built or when it would happen, and Apple didn’t provide further comment to the press at the time. Shortly after, Foxconn, Apple’s main manufacturing partner, said it would open a $10 billion plant in Wisconsin that will eventually employ more than 13,000 people — which President Trump touted as a sign of his ability to get companies to reinvest in U.S. manufacturing. In exchange, the Taiwanese electronics manufacturing giant is getting a $3 billion taxpayer-funded incentive and subsidies package. An analysis has shown the state won’t break even on its Foxconn investment until 2042 . Apple employs 84,000 employees across the U.S., meaning the tech giant plans to blow past the 100,000-employee mark in the next five years. It's the largest technology employer in Silicon Valley , with about 25,000 employees in the region. No. 2 is Google and parent company Alphabet, with about 20,000 employees. So far, Apple has released a handful of details about where its planned $350 million investment will come from in that time. Among those investments: $75 billion in already-planned capital expenditures, investments in manufacturing and tax payments;$55 billion spent with U.S. suppliers and manufacturers in 2018; $38 billion of its tax payments will be from repatriation tax payments – likely the largest of its kind ever made, Apple touted Wednesday; $30 billion in capital expenditures and job creation at existing campuses and a new one; $10 billion in capital expenditures in data centers. (Currently the company has data centers and facilities in North Carolina, Oregon, Nevada, Arizona and just announced a project in Iowa); $5 billion in its Advanced Manufacturing Fund to support innovation among U.S. manufacturers. Apple's new headquarters in Cupertino, California, opened last year. The 2.8 million-square-foot campus will house 13,000 workers and is estimated to have cost $5 billion to build. Just last fall, another booming West Coast company set out to find a home for its second headquarters. Seattle-based Amazon.com Inc. (Nasdaq: AMZN) solicited bids to help it select a North American city to house its proposed $5 billion second headquarters, which could employ up to 50,000 people in high-paying, tech-savvy jobs. It received 238 bids from 54 states, provinces, districts and territories cities in the U.S. and Canada. In addition to the Greater Houston Partnership's bid on behalf of the Bayou City , local developers like Midway Cos. with its East River property and McCord Development and its Generation Park project also have been targeting Amazon. Amazon.com officials say they expect to make a decision on the HQ2 real estate search sometime this year.
